```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
strava_runs <- read_csv("data/strava_runs.csv")
```

```{r}
data_5k_10k <- strava_runs %>%
  mutate(
    event = case_when(
      distance..m. > 4998 & distance..m. < 5015  ~ "5k",
      distance..m. > 9998 & distance..m. < 10015 ~ "10k",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(event))
```


## Exercise 1

When you fill the missing part, remove the # symbol before running the code chunk and eval=FALSE

```{r ex1a, out.width="80%"}
data_5k_10k %>%
  filter(gender == "M") %>%
  filter(!is.na(average.heart.rate..bpm.)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = average.heart.rate..bpm.)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  labs(
    title = "Average heart rate for male runners",
    x = "Average heart rate (bpm)",
    y = "Number of runs"
  )

data_5k_10k %>%
  filter(gender == "M") %>%
  summarise(
    n = sum(!is.na(average.heart.rate..bpm.)),
    mean_bpm = mean(average.heart.rate..bpm., na.rm = TRUE),
    median_bpm = median(average.heart.rate..bpm., na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_bpm = sd(average.heart.rate..bpm., na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```
The histogram is approximately unimodal and bell-shaped, with a main peak
around 145–150 bpm. The mean (147.94 bpm) and median (147.90 bpm) are
almost identical, supporting an approximately symmetric distribution.
The standard deviation is 17.22 bpm. There is no clear evidence of
separate clusters in this histogram. These statistics are based on
252 runs with non-missing heart rate measurements.


```{r ex1b, out.width="80%"}
# Write your code for Ex1b here
data_5k_10k %>%
  filter(gender == "F") %>%
  filter(!is.na(average.heart.rate..bpm.)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = average.heart.rate..bpm.)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  labs(
    title = "Average heart rate for female runners",
    x = "Average heart rate (bpm)",
    y = "Number of runs"
  )

data_5k_10k %>%
  filter(gender == "F") %>%
  summarise(
    n = sum(!is.na(average.heart.rate..bpm.)),
    mean_bpm = mean(average.heart.rate..bpm., na.rm = TRUE),
    median_bpm = median(average.heart.rate..bpm., na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_bpm = sd(average.heart.rate..bpm., na.rm = TRUE)
  )




```


The female histogram has several peaks and is less smooth than the male
histogram. Female runs have a higher mean heart rate (155.68 bpm) than
male runs (147.94 bpm). The standard deviation is smaller for females
(13.22 versus 17.22 bpm), so their heart rates are less spread out.
However, the two distributions overlap.


## Exercise 2


# Write your code to answer exercise 2a here
```{r ex2, out.width="80%"}
data_5k_10k %>%
  filter(!is.na(gender)) %>%
  mutate(
    pace = (elapsed.time..s. / 60) / (distance..m. / 1000),
    event = factor(event, levels = c("5k", "10k"))
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = event, y = pace)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ gender, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Running pace for 5k and 10k runs",
    subtitle = "F = Female, M = Male; lower pace means faster running",
    x = "Run distance",
    y = "Pace (minutes per km)"
  )



```

Male runs have a lower median pace than female runs at both distances,
so they are generally faster in this dataset. For both genders, 10k runs
have a slightly lower median pace than 5k runs. The 5k runs show more
variation, with some much slower runs.



## Exercise 3

```{r ex3, out.width = "80%"}
# Write your code to answer exercise 3 here
runner_groups <- strava_runs %>%
  group_by(athlete) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_distance = mean(distance..m., na.rm = TRUE) / 1000
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    runner_type = case_when(
      mean_distance > 13 ~ "Long-distance runner",
      mean_distance < 7 ~ "Short-distance runner",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(runner_type))

runner_data <- strava_runs %>%
  inner_join(runner_groups, by = "athlete") %>%
  mutate(
    distance_km = distance..m. / 1000,
    speed = distance..m. / elapsed.time..s.
  )

ggplot(
  runner_data,
  aes(x = distance_km, y = speed, colour = runner_type)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Long-distance runner" = "orange",
      "Short-distance runner" = "forestgreen"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Speed vs Distance for Long- and Short-Distance Runners",
    subtitle = "Grouped by runners' average distance: >13 km vs <7 km",
    x = "Run distance (km)",
    y = "Run average speed (m/s)",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")




```


Long-distance runners tend to run faster than short-distance runners
at the same distance. Both lines slope downwards, but the decrease
is greater for short-distance runners. This suggests that the two
groups have different speed patterns, although their results overlap.

## Exercise 4

```{r ex4, out.width = "80%"}
# Write your code to answer exercise 4 here
gender_means <- strava_runs %>%
  filter(!is.na(gender)) %>%
  group_by(gender) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_distance = mean(distance..m., na.rm = TRUE) / 1000,
    mean_time = mean(elapsed.time..s., na.rm = TRUE) / 60
  )

gender_means

gender_means %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mean_distance, mean_time),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "mean_value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    measure = factor(
      measure,
      levels = c("mean_distance", "mean_time"),
      labels = c("Mean distance (km)", "Mean time (minutes)")
    )
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = gender, y = mean_value, fill = gender)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free_y", nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean running distance and time by gender",
    subtitle = "F = Female, M = Male",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Mean value",
    fill = "Gender"
  )




```

Male runs have a longer mean distance (10.61 km) than female runs
(9.70 km). However, the mean elapsed time is almost the same for both
genders, at about 62.4 minutes.
